newsitem.title: USA: Hearings to disclose cigarette contents to start.
newsitem.headline: Hearings to disclose cigarette contents to start.

text.p: Efforts by four tobacco companies to block public hearings on the contents of individual brands of cigarettes went up in smoke Wednesday when a federal judge ruled the hearings could go on as planned.

The Massachusetts Department of Public Health hearings, set to begin here Thursday morning, are part of a process to design regulations that will require all companies that sell cigarettes and smokeless tobacco in the state to disclose the ingredients by brand by July 1, 1997.
Philip Morris Cos. Inc., R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. and Lorillard Tobacco Co. tried unsuccessfully to block the hearings from going forward.
The companies filed suit shortly after Massachusetts passed the law last summer that would require them to disclose their brands' contents, seeking to have the measure declared unconstitutional.

The firms' lawyer Harry Dinger told U.S. District Judge George O'Toole that the hearings presented his clients with "a Hobson's choice... If we participate, as a practical matter, it will be necessary to disclose the information we brought this action to protect."
Massachusetts Assistant Attorney General Thomas Barnico argued that the tobacco firms had misread the regulations and that the hearings were public discourse.
"They have a choice, to put it simply, whether to participate or not," Barnico said.
O'Toole, who did not rule on the law's constitutionality, said, "I'm not persuaded there is irreparable harm..." in denying the companies' motion to block the hearings.

The four companies plan on submitting just four pages of written testimony at the hearings, a spokesman for the firms, David Remes, said before the court hearing. They have until Feb. 21 to submit further written comment.

But in their testimony to be submitted Thursday, the four call the law and the hearings unconstitutional, unlawful and inappropriate "while the manufacturers' legal challenge to the statute is pending."

The companies argue that the "proposed nicotine reporting provisions would not produce or lead to ratings that 'accurately predict nicotine intake for average consumers.' They would merely produce, for each brand, smoking-machine test ratings that are higher than those produced under the current FTC (Federal Trade Commission) test method..."

Department Deputy Commissioner Greg Connolly told reporters Thursday's hearing would deal with how much tar and nicotine smokers receive from different cigarette brands. Friday's hearing will discuss cigarette ingredients, he said.
The American Cancer Society and the American Lung Association are both expected to testify Thursday, a department spokeswoman said.
